paragraphs: Led by Hector, the Trojans and their allies break through the wall.

While the son of Menoetius tended Eurypylus’s wound inside the tent, the Argives and Trojans went on fighting desperately. But the trench and the high wall above it were not going to hold the Trojans back much longer. The Achaeans had built the wall to protect their ships, and had dug the trench all around it to keep both the ships and the rich spoils they had taken safe. But they had never offered a great sacrifice to the gods. Because it was built without the immortals’ consent, it did not last. As long as Hector lived, Achilles kept up his anger, and Priam’s city stayed unsacked, the great wall of the Achaeans stood firm. Then the bravest of the Trojans died, and many of the Argives too, though some were still alive. In the tenth year the city was sacked, and the Argives sailed home to their own country. After that Poseidon and Apollo made a plan to destroy the wall. They turned the streams of all the rivers that run from Mount Ida to the sea onto it: the Rhesus, the Heptaporus, the Caresus, the Rhodius, the Grenicus, the Aesopus, and goodly Scamander, and the Simois, where many a shield and helmet had fallen and many a hero of the race of demigods had bitten the dust. Phoebus Apollo brought the mouths of all these rivers together and sent them flowing against the wall for nine days. Zeus rained the whole time, so that the sea would wash the wall away sooner. Poseidon himself, trident in hand, looked over the work. He threw into the sea all the foundations of beams and stones that the Achaeans had laid with so much toil. He leveled everything along the mighty stream of the Hellespont, and when the wall was swept away he spread a great beach of sand over the place where it had stood. Then he turned the rivers back into their old channels.

That was what Poseidon and Apollo would do in later times. For now, battle and turmoil still raged around the wall, and its timbers rang under the blows that rained on them. Cowed by the scourge of Zeus, the Argives were penned in at their ships, afraid of Hector, the mighty minister of Rout, who fought as before with the force and fury of a whirlwind. A lion or wild boar turns fiercely on the dogs and men who attack him. They stand together in a solid wall and shower javelins at him as they face him. His courage is not shaken at all, but his high spirit will be the death of him. Many times he charges at his pursuers to scatter them, and each time they give way. In the same way Hector went about among the host, urging his men on and calling them to cross the trench.

But the horses did not dare. They stood neighing at the edge, because the width of it frightened them. They could neither jump it nor cross it. It had overhanging banks all the way around on both sides, and above these were the sharp stakes that the sons of the Achaeans had planted close and strong to guard against anyone who attacked. A horse could not get down into it and pull his chariot after him. The men on foot, though, kept trying with all their strength. Then Polydamas went up to Hector and said, “Hector, and you other captains of the Trojans and allies, it is madness to try to drive our horses across the trench. It will be very hard to cross, because it is full of sharp stakes, and beyond them is the wall. The horses cannot get down into it, and they would be no use if they did. It is also a narrow place, and we would come to harm. If great Zeus really means to help the Trojans, and in his anger will utterly destroy the Achaeans, I would gladly see them perish here and now, far from Argos. But suppose they rally, and we are driven back from the ships in a jumble into the trench. Then not one man will get back to the city to tell the tale. So let us all do as I say. Let our squires hold our horses by the trench, and let us follow Hector in a body on foot, in full armor. If the day of their doom is near, the Achaeans will not be able to stand against us.”

So Polydamas spoke, and Hector liked what he said. He sprang to the ground in full armor, and when the other Trojans saw him do it, they all left their chariots too. Each man handed his horses to his charioteer, to hold them ready for him at the trench. Then they formed into companies, got themselves ready, and followed their leaders in five bodies. The ones who went with Hector and Polydamas were the bravest and the most numerous, and the most determined to break through the wall and fight at the ships. Cebriones joined them as third in command, since Hector had left his chariot in the care of a less valiant soldier. Paris, Alcathous and Agenor led the next company. Helenus and Deiphobus, two sons of Priam, led the third, and with them was the hero Asius, son of Hyrtacus, whose great black horses of the breed from the river Selleis had carried him from Arisbe. Aeneas, the valiant son of Anchises, led the fourth, together with the two sons of Antenor, Archelochus and Acamas, men well versed in every art of war. Sarpedon was captain of the allies. He took with him Glaucus and Asteropaeus, whom he considered the most valiant after himself, for he was far the best of them all. They helped one another put on their ox-hide shields, and then charged straight at the Danaans. They were sure the Danaans could not hold out any longer, and that they themselves would now fall on the ships.

The rest of the Trojans and their allies now followed the advice of Polydamas. But Asius, son of Hyrtacus, would not leave his horses and his squire behind. In his foolhardiness he took them on toward the ships, and it brought him to his end. He was never to return to wind-beaten Ilium, boasting in his chariot and his horses. Before that, death with its ill-omened name overshadowed him, and he fell by the spear of Idomeneus, the noble son of Deucalion. He had driven toward the left wing of the ships, the way the Achaeans used to come back from the plain with their chariots and horses. He drove there and found the gates standing wide open, with the great bar down, because the gatemen kept them open to let in any comrades who might be fleeing toward the ships. Asius steered his horses there on purpose, and his men followed with a loud cry. They were sure the Achaeans could not hold out any longer and that they would now fall on the ships. They little knew that at the gates they would find two of the bravest chieftains, proud sons of the fighting Lapithae. One was Polypoetes, the mighty son of Pirithous, and the other was Leonteus, peer of murderous Ares. These two stood before the gates like two high oak trees on the mountains, which tower up from their wide-spreading roots and battle the wind and rain year after year. In the same way these two men awaited the onset of great Asius with confidence, without flinching. The Trojans raised a loud battle cry and made straight for the wall, holding their shields of dry ox-hide above their heads. They were led by Asius and by Iamenus, Orestes, Adamas the son of Asius, Thoon and Oenomaus. For a while the two defenders stayed inside and called on the Achaeans to stand firm in defense of their ships. But then they saw the Trojans attacking the wall, while the Danaans cried out for help and were routed. They rushed outside and fought in front of the gates like two wild boars on the mountains. The boars wait for the attack of men and dogs, and charging at them from either side they break down the wood all around, tearing it up by the roots, and one can hear the clattering of their tusks until someone hits them and ends them. So the gleaming bronze rattled about the breasts of the two men as the weapons fell on them. They fought with great fury, trusting in their own prowess and in the men on the wall above them. These threw great stones at the attackers to defend themselves, their tents and their ships. The stones fell as thick as flakes of snow, when a fierce blast drives them from the dark clouds and showers them down in sheets upon the earth. So the weapons fell from the hands of Trojans and Achaeans alike. Helmet and shield rang out as the great stones rained on them. Asius, son of Hyrtacus, cried out in dismay and struck his two thighs. “Father Zeus,” he cried, “truly you too are altogether given to lying. I was sure the Argive heroes could not withstand us. But they are like slim-waisted wasps, or bees that have their nests in the rocks by the wayside. These do not leave the holes they have built undefended, but fight for their little ones against anyone who would take them. In the same way these men, though they are only two, will not be driven from the gates. They stand firm to kill or be killed.”

He spoke, but he did not change the mind of Zeus, whose plan at that time was to give glory to Hector. Meanwhile the rest of the Trojans were fighting at the other gates. I, however, am no god, and cannot tell about all these things, for the battle raged everywhere around the stone wall like a fiery furnace. The Argives, beaten though they were, were forced to defend their ships, and all the gods who were defending the Achaeans were vexed in spirit. But the Lapithae kept on fighting with all their might.

Then Polypoetes, mighty son of Pirithous, hit Damasus on his cheek-pierced helmet with a spear. The helmet did not protect him. The point of the spear went through it and broke the bone, so that the brain inside was scattered about, and he died fighting. Polypoetes then killed Pylon and Ormenus. Leonteus, of the race of Ares, killed Hippomachus the son of Antimachus, by striking him on the girdle with his spear. Then he drew his sword and sprang first on Antiphates, whom he killed in close combat, and who fell face upward on the ground. After him he killed Menon, Iamenus and Orestes, and laid them low one after another.

While the two Lapiths were busy stripping the armor from these heroes, the young men led by Polydamas and Hector were still standing by the trench, unsure what to do. These were the greater part and the most valiant of those trying to break through the wall and set fire to the ships. They had seen a sign from heaven when they tried to cross. An eagle soared along the left wing of their host, carrying a monstrous blood-red snake in its talons, still alive and struggling to escape. The snake had not given up its revenge. It twisted and wriggled backward until it struck the bird that held it, on the neck and breast. In pain, the bird let it fall into the middle of the host, and then flew off down the wind with a sharp cry. The Trojans were struck with terror when they saw the snake, a portent of aegis-bearing Zeus, writhing in the midst of them. Polydamas went up to Hector and said, “Hector, at our councils of war you are always rebuking me, even when I speak wisely. It seems it is not right, you say, for one of the people to cross your will, either in the field or at the council board. You want them to support you always. Still, I will say what I think is best. Let us not go on now to fight the Danaans at their ships. I know what will happen, if this soaring eagle that skirted the left wing of our host with a monstrous blood-red snake in its talons (the snake still alive) was really sent as an omen to the Trojans as they tried to cross the trench. The eagle let go her hold. She did not manage to take the snake home to her little ones, and so it will be with us. Even if by a mighty effort we break through the gates and wall of the Achaeans, and they give way before us, we shall still not return in good order the way we came. We shall leave many a man behind, whom the Achaeans will put to death in defense of their ships. This is how any seer who was expert in these matters, and trusted by the people, would read the portent.”

Hector looked fiercely at him and said, “Polydamas, I do not like your reading. You can find a better thing to say than this, if you try. But if you have spoken in good earnest, then heaven has robbed you of your reason. You would have me pay no heed to the counsels of Zeus, or to the promises he made me, when he bowed his head in confirmation. You tell me to be ruled instead by the flight of wild birds. What do I care whether they fly toward dawn or dark, or whether they are on my right hand or my left? Let us put our trust rather in the counsel of great Zeus, king of mortals and immortals. There is one omen, and one only: that a man should fight for his country. Why are you so afraid? Even if all the rest of us are killed at the ships of the Argives, you are not likely to be killed yourself, because you are neither steadfast nor courageous. If you will not fight, or if you talk others out of fighting, you shall fall at once before my spear.”
